analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefit checks and starts taxing wages above the annual earnings cap.
analysis.headline: Senator Schatz introduced the bill on December 11, 2025 with one Democratic cosponsor, and it has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises Social Security benefits across the board. It lifts the replacement rate in the lowest bracket of the benefit formula from 90 to 95 cents per dollar, recomputes checks for people already retired so they get a share of the increase, and switches annual cost-of-living adjustments to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers that tracks retiree spending. To help pay for it, it begins counting a share of wages above the annual taxable cap (about $176,000 in 2025) as Social Security wages, though high earners get only a small credit toward benefits for those extra taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Current retirees get larger checks starting January 2026 through the benefit recomputation, and no one's check can be cut by the recomputation. Lower- and middle-wage workers get higher benefits when they retire, because more of their earnings are replaced at the higher 95 percent rate. All beneficiaries get cost-of-living adjustments based on a retiree-specific price index, which reflects the heavy share retirees spend on health care and housing. The bill's stated aim is also to strengthen the program's finances for future generations by extending payroll taxes above the cap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the replacement rate in the lowest bracket of the Social Security benefit formula from 90 percent to 95 percent, so a larger share of every worker's first dollars of earnings comes back as benefits.
The Commissioner of Social Security must recompute benefits for people already on the rolls effective January 2026, and the recomputation can only raise a check, never lower it.

Annual cost-of-living adjustments would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish to track the spending patterns of people at retirement age, whose costs (especially health care) differ from the index now used for Social Security.

Beginning in 2026, a share of wages above the annual contribution and benefit base counts as taxable Social Security wages under a set schedule running through 2029, extending the payroll tax to earnings above the cap for employees, employers, and the self-employed.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people with earnings above the annual taxable cap (about $176,000 in 2025) would pay Social Security tax on a share of their above-cap earnings, with self-employed people paying both the employee and employer shares. High-wage employers would owe the employer share on above-cap wages. Because only 5 percent of above-cap earnings counts toward benefits, high earners pay in far more than they get back.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: High earners pay Social Security tax on above-cap wages but only 5 percent of those surplus earnings counts toward their future benefits, so the bill breaks the usual link between what top earners pay in and what they get back.
Self-employed people with high incomes are hit hardest, since they pay the combined employee and employer payroll tax rate on above-cap net earnings.

As drafted, the share of above-cap wages counted as taxable starts at 80 percent in 2026 and steps down to zero percent in 2030 under the bill's own schedule, while the benefit increases are permanent, leaving the long-term financing of the expansion unclear.
High-wage employers, including smaller professional firms, would owe the 6.2 percent employer share on above-cap wages, a new payroll cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For retirees and future beneficiaries the gains are concrete and start quickly: a higher replacement rate in the bottom bracket, a recomputed check for current beneficiaries, and a cost-of-living index built around retiree expenses. The cost falls on the highest earners, who pay taxes on above-cap earnings that buy them little benefit. The bill's biggest weakness is its own financing schedule: as written, the taxed share of above-cap wages steps down to zero by 2030 while the benefit increases continue, so the long-term solvency math the bill promises is not settled by the text provided.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred straight to the Senate Finance Committee, and nothing else has happened to it yet.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill in the Senate on December 11, 2025.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which handles Social Security and tax legislation.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or other action has been recorded since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nothing has changed: the bill has not moved since referral, so current benefit levels and the current payroll tax cap remain exactly as they are, which in itself preserves the tax treatment of the highest earners.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: high earners keep current tax treatment

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats are attached so far and no vote has occurred, so any partisan split on the bill has yet to form.

industries.note: The bill starts applying the Social Security payroll tax to wages above the annual cap, so the highest earners pay more in taxes that fund benefit increases for everyone else. Their interest in blocking or slowing the bill runs against the interest of beneficiaries.

industries.industry: High-income self-employed professionals and business owners
industries.note: Self-employed people pay both the employee and employer payroll tax shares, so physicians, lawyers, consultants, and owners with above-cap net earnings face the largest new tax under the bill.
Employers would owe the 6.2 percent employer share on the taxable portion of above-cap wages, adding a payroll cost for firms with highly paid staffs.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress runs through January 2027. With one cosponsor and no committee action in the days since introduction, the bill would need the Finance Committee to schedule a hearing and markup and then the full Senate to take it up — steps that most Social Security expansion bills referred to committee never reach. Unless it picks up substantially more support, the likely path is that it sits in committee and dies at the end of the session.
